questions.problem:
Let $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{y}^{2}z,$ where $x=3t,$ $y=t-s$ and $z=2st.$ Given that

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡3t+{c}_{1}s{t}^{2}+{c}_{2}{s}^{2}t+{c}_{3}{s}^{3},
$$

find the value of ${c}_{1}+{c}_{2}+{c}_{3}.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14199265/assets/b593a1b60fe8c1aef2c5c229ff426db350e6296b9ecb767494283f0fa3342072.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2yz,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}={y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡3t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2(t-s)(2st)=4s{t}^{2}-4{s}^{2}t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =(t-s)^{2}={t}^{2}-2st+{s}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =3, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =1, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂t} & =2s.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =(-\operatorname{sin}⁡3t)\cdot 3+(4s{t}^{2}-4{s}^{2}t)\cdot 1+({t}^{2}-2st+{s}^{2})\cdot 2s \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡3t+4s{t}^{2}-4{s}^{2}t+2s{t}^{2}-4{s}^{2}t+2{s}^{3} \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡3t+6s{t}^{2}-8{s}^{2}t+2{s}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, ${c}_{1}=6,$ ${c}_{2}=-8$ and ${c}_{3}=2,$ and therefore

$$
{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}+{c}_{3}=6+(-8)+2=0.
$$

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-4\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2(2st)=4st, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =2t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =2st.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s} \\  & =(4st)(2t)+(-4)(2st) \\  & =8s{t}^{2}-8st \\  & =8st(t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(st), \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(st).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =s\operatorname{cos}⁡(st), \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =-s\operatorname{sin}⁡(st).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t} \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡(st))(s\operatorname{cos}⁡(st))+(\operatorname{sin}⁡(st))(-s\operatorname{sin}⁡(st)) \\  & =s{cos}^{2}⁡(st)-s{sin}^{2}⁡(st) \\  & =s({cos}^{2}⁡(st)-{sin}^{2}⁡(st)) \\  & =s\operatorname{cos}⁡(2st).\end{aligned}
$$

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{x+y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{x+y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{x+{e}^{2x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2{e}^{2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{x+{e}^{2x}}+\frac{1}{x+{e}^{2x}}\cdot 2{e}^{2x} \\  & =\frac{1}{x+{e}^{2x}}+\frac{2{e}^{2x}}{x+{e}^{2x}} \\  & =\frac{1+2{e}^{2x}}{x+{e}^{2x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-1,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-1,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & ={e}^{s}, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =1, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂s} & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =(-1)\cdot {e}^{s}+(-1)\cdot 1+(1)\cdot (-1) \\  & =-{e}^{s}-2.\end{aligned}
$$
